hints: Focus on what an acceptor needs for a dative bond, an empty orbital that can take both electrons from the donor.
Check each species for an incomplete octet or empty 1s orbital, starting with boron in $\text{BF}_3$ which has only 6 electrons around it.
Now test $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3^+$ the same way and see if all three are electron deficient enough to accept a pair.
walkthrough:
**Recall the rule for accepting**

Think of a coordinate bond as donor provides both electrons, acceptor provides an empty orbital. So ask, does this species have room for two more electrons?

Rule:
$$\text{donor (lone pair)} + \text{acceptor (empty orbital)} \rightarrow \text{dative bond}$$

**Test 1: $\text{BF}_3$**

Boron is in Group 13 with 3 outer electrons. In $\text{BF}_3$ it forms 3 bonds, so only 6 electrons in its outer shell, not 8. That leaves an empty p orbital ready to accept, for example from $\text{NH}_3$ to make $\text{F}_3\text{B} \leftarrow \text{NH}_3$. So 1 is correct.

**Test 2: $\text{H}^+$**

$\text{H}^+$ is just a proton with an empty 1s orbital and no electrons at all. It loves to accept a lone pair, for example:
$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$$
So 2 is correct.

**Test 3: $\text{CH}_3^+$**

Carbon normally wants 8 electrons. In $\text{CH}_3^+$ it has only 3 bonds, so 6 electrons, and a positive charge showing electron deficiency. It has an empty p orbital and readily accepts a pair, for example from $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. So 3 is correct.

**Conclude the combination**

Since 1, 2 and 3 can all accept a lone pair, the correct combination is 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct. All three are electron deficient acceptors. $\text{BF}_3$ has an incomplete octet on B, $\text{H}^+$ has an empty 1s orbital, and $\text{CH}_3^+$ has only 6 electrons on C with an empty p orbital.
options.B: Incorrect. This would mean 1 and 2 only. Students choose this if they forget that the methyl carbocation $\text{CH}_3^+$ is also electron deficient and a classic Lewis acid, just like $\text{BF}_3$.
options.C: Incorrect. This would mean 2 and 3 only. Students choose this if they think $\text{BF}_3$ is stable and full because fluorine is very electronegative, forgetting boron still has only a sextet.
options.D: Incorrect. This would mean 1 only. Students choose this if they only remember the famous $\text{BF}_3$ example and miss that any cation with an empty orbital, like $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3^+$, is an excellent acceptor.
